The document is Jonathan Swift’s *A Modest Proposal*, not a literal policy memo. So the question is whether its “explanation” holds up. Literally, no: eating poor children is monstrous, illegal, and economically self-defeating. Satirically, yes: it works by taking the dehumanizing logic of colonial and landlord economics to its logical conclusion.

**What does the work**

The deadpan political arithmetic is the engine. Swift counts 120,000 poor children, reserves 20,000 for breeding, sells 100,000, prices a child at 10 shillings, costs at 2, profits at 8, and adds £50,000 to the national stock. This mimics the “projectors” of his day and makes cannibalism sound like a ledger entry. The horror comes from the calm.

The moral inversion is the hinge: “landlords… have already devoured most of the parents, seem to have the best title to the children.” The proposal is not a new atrocity but a literal version of existing exploitation. That is the satirical point.

The real grievances are the actual argument: Popery, absentees, tithes, foreign luxuries, Irish factions, landlord cruelty, cheating shopkeepers. The list of “other expedients” near the end—tax absentees, buy Irish goods, reject foreign luxury, cure pride, practice parsimony, love your country, quit factions, don’t sell your country and conscience, teach landlords mercy, make shopkeepers honest—is what Swift is really proposing. He says: if you reject these, you have no standing to reject my scheme. That is the explanation that holds up.

The disinterested narrator—“I have no children… wife past child-bearing”—is a standard pamphlet pose. It makes the speaker seem public-spirited while proposing infanticide. It works as irony.

**What is loose**

The pseudo-authorities are flimsy: “a very knowing American of my acquaintance,” “famous Psalmanaazor,” “a grave author, an eminent French physician.” These are vague or dubious. They are meant to be flimsy, but they loosen the argument if read literally.

The numbers are arbitrary. 1.5 million souls, 200,000 breeders, 30,000 able to maintain, 50,000 miscarriages/deaths, 120,000 children—plausible enough to parody, but not empirically grounded. The 28-pound one-year-old is high. The assumption that one male serves four females is arbitrary and offensive.

The economics have gaps. Flooding the market with 100,000 carcasses would crash the price. The proposal ignores human capital: children are future laborers, taxpayers, soldiers, breeders. It assumes mothers will sell without resistance, landlords will become popular, taverns will boom. These are satirical exaggerations, not predictions.

The venison digression—using 12-to-14-year-olds as deer substitute—dilutes the focus. It makes the original seem moderate, but it is a loose refinement.

The Lent/Popish argument is bigoted and factually shaky. It serves to expose anti-Catholic prejudice, but it is not a serious demographic claim.

**What would test it**

Historical demography and economy: How many poor were there in Ireland in 1729? What were rents, exports, absentee flows? Did landlords extract enough to cause starvation? The historical record largely supports Swift’s exploitation critique.

The alternative remedies: Were taxing absentees, buying Irish goods, and landlord mercy feasible? Did any attempts work? This tests whether Swift’s real explanation is practical or just moral outrage.

Reader response: Did contemporaries read it as satire? Did it change policy? Did it persuade or only outrage? That tests rhetorical effectiveness.

Moral logic: Does the satire make readers feel complicit? If readers laugh and then do nothing, the explanation holds up as diagnosis but fails as cure.

Economic modeling: A simple model shows that consuming children reduces future productive capacity. That is a test the literal proposal fails—which is the point.

So the explanation holds up as satire: its target is not the poor but the comfortable who treat them as livestock. Its loose parts are intentional or symptomatic of the genre. The test is whether the real remedies were ignored—and they were.
